candidates.attacker_control: The class name and its String argument are length-prefixed UTF strings read directly from the wire packet by tightUnmarsalThrowable/looseUnmarsalThrowable (BaseDataStreamMarshaller.java lines 190-192 and 511-513). Any peer able to open a TCP connection to an OpenWire connector fully controls both values; the shipped activemq.xml exposes OpenWire on 0.0.0.0:61616 (activemq-all/src/main/resources/activemq.xml line 100; same in assembly/src/release/conf/activemq.xml line 113). No broker-side credentials, handshake or pre-existing connection state are needed.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Searched for any guard in the openwire packages: no Throwable.class.isAssignableFrom check, allow-list, or class-name validation exists (isAssignableFrom usages found only in unrelated XPathExpression/JNDI/IntrospectionSupport/JAXB code). Confirmed the cast to Throwable happens after constructor.newInstance, so a non-Throwable class is still constructed before the ClassCastException is swallowed. Confirmed both tight and loose unmarshal paths call createThrowable and that the default wire version (12) plus legacy v2-v8 include the same method. Confirmed the call is on the transport read path (TcpTransport.readCommand) before broker-level authentication (SimpleAuthenticationBroker.addConnection) and before command processing (Response.visit returns null), and that ExceptionResponse type 31 is registered in the marshaller table. Confirmed the shipped default configuration exposes the OpenWire connector without requiring prior authentication. Considered the possibility that a negotiated WireFormatInfo could disable vulnerable parsing; it cannot, because both encodings reach createThrowable.
candidates.impact: Unauthenticated remote code execution in the broker JVM (or in any JVM that deserializes OpenWire Throwables, e.g. clients receiving crafted error/poison-cause fields) as the process user: full compromise of the broker host, message confidentiality/integrity loss, and pivot potential. Even without a usable gadget, it is an unauthenticated arbitrary-class-instantiation primitive driven entirely by network input. Successful exploitation depends on the classpath containing a class whose String constructor has harmful side effects; the code makes no attempt to constrain this.
candidates.prerequisites: Network reachability to an OpenWire transport (default tcp://0.0.0.0:61616); no authentication, since unmarshalling occurs on the transport reader thread before the broker processes ConnectionInfo and calls AuthenticationBroker (SimpleAuthenticationBroker.addConnection lines 68-74 performs authentication only when ConnectionInfo is handled). A class with a public String constructor and dangerous side effects must exist on the broker JVM classpath; the standard distribution bundles Spring and other libraries, which is the condition that turns the instantiation primitive into code execution (classpath-dependent). Default wire version is 12 (CommandTypes.PROTOCOL_VERSION = 12; OpenWireFormatFactory lines 34-38 default tight encoding on), and ExceptionResponse/ConnectionError/MessageAck all carry Throwable fields through this code path.
candidates.root_cause: BaseDataStreamMarshaller.createThrowable(String className, String message) trusts the class name decoded from an OpenWire Throwable field: it does Class.forName(className, false, loader), obtains the public String constructor and calls constructor.newInstance(message) without verifying that the class is a Throwable or belongs to a safe allow-list. The constructor body (and class initialization) executes before the result is cast to Throwable, and the catch(Throwable) swallows the resulting ClassCastException, so any class with a side-effecting String constructor on the classpath is instantiated from attacker-supplied data. The same unvalidated pattern is duplicated across all openwire version packages (v1-v12 and legacy v2-v8).
candidates.title: Pre-auth attacker-controlled class instantiation in OpenWire Throwable unmarshalling (createThrowable) enables remote code execution
candidates.trace: Remote bytes -> TcpTransport.doRun/readCommand (TcpTransport.java 230-241) -> OpenWireFormat.unmarshal (OpenWireFormat.java 264-279) -> doUnmarshal reads the data-structure type byte and dispatches to the registered marshaller (OpenWireFormat.java 354-368) -> ExceptionResponseMarshaller.tightUnmarshal calls tightUnmarsalThrowable (ExceptionResponseMarshaller.java 65-69) -> BaseDataStreamMarshaller.tightUnmarsalThrowable reads attacker class name + message and calls createThrowable (v12 BaseDataStreamMarshaller.java 190-192) -> createThrowable resolves the class and invokes its String constructor (v12 BaseDataStreamMarshaller.java 227-235). Response.visit() returns null, so the command does not even need to be meaningfully processed by the broker; the side effect occurs during unmarshalling. The loose-encoding path (line 508-513) and the legacy/openwire v1-v11 copies are identically affected, so downgrading the negotiated wire version does not mitigate.
candidates.unverified: No code was executed and no payload was sent; I did not build or run the broker. Whether a specific deployment has a suitable String-constructor gadget on its classpath is deployment-dependent and was not verified. I did not attempt to enumerate all possible gadget classes. The precise fix history/CVE label for this snapshot was not consulted (no external data or labels used).
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-502 Deserialization of Untrusted Data / CWE-470 Unsafe Reflection (attacker-controlled class instantiation)

coverage_summary: Scope: 2,691 visible text files under the ActiveMQ 5.15.12 tree (get_source_scope reports 0 excluded by size/name/symlink; binary-like files are skipped by the tools). Test sources and .jspf includes are not present in the snapshot. I reviewed remotely reachable paths in depth: activemq-client OpenWire marshalling (all version packages and the legacy module), transports (tcp, http/xstream/text wire formats), broker transport/connection and authentication/authorization classes, activemq-web and activemq-web-console (JSPs, tag files, servlets, filters, controllers), activemq-jaas login modules, blob strategies, jdbc-store SQL construction, and the shipped default configurations. Sampled but did not exhaustively review: activemq-broker region/Queue/dispatch internals, kahadb/leveldb stores, mqtt/stomp/amqp protocol converters, console tooling, OSGi/Spring/Karaf integration, and the partition and shiro modules.
limitations: No code was executed, built, or tested; all findings are static source analysis and none is runtime-confirmed.
The RCE candidate's practical exploitability depends on the broker classpath containing a suitable String-constructor class; I could not enumerate the runtime classpath from the snapshot.

The snapshot omits all test sources and .jspf includes, so behavior could not be cross-checked against tests and one JSP include referenced by the web console (WEB-INF/jspf/headertags.jspf) is not visible.
A large repository (2,691 files) cannot be fully reviewed file-by-file in this run; modules listed in the coverage summary were only sampled, so additional issues may exist there.
No external CVE/ground-truth/patch data was consulted, by instruction; the report therefore describes source-level defects rather than mapping them to specific advisories.

rejected_leads.lead: Reflected XSS in the admin web console: message.jsp emits the request parameter ${requestContext.messageQuery.JMSDestination} unescaped inside a JavaScript string in the always-rendered <script> block (activemq-web-console/src/main/webapp/message.jsp line 238-239). The parameter is bound to DestinationFacade.jmsDestination with only a trim (DestinationFacade.java 90-95) via ApplicationContextFilter.bindRequestBean (ApplicationContextFilter.java 195-199), and an attacker can reach the sink without a valid message id because the c:choose empty branch still renders the script.
rejected_leads.reason: Real input-handling defect, but impact is a reflected XSS in an authenticated admin session that requires the victim to open a crafted URL; substantially lower impact and more conditional than the pre-auth RCE candidate, so it was not selected. It remains a plausible separately tracked web-console XSS issue.

rejected_leads.lead: Unbounded allocation in TextWireFormat.unmarshal: 'int length = in.readInt(); byte[] utf8 = new byte[length];' uses the attacker-controlled 32-bit length with no bound check (activemq-http/src/main/java/org/apache/activemq/transport/util/TextWireFormat.java 51-57).
rejected_leads.reason: At most a memory-exhaustion DoS and only reachable when a text-based wire format is configured; not remotely reachable under the default OpenWire configuration, so it was not selected.

rejected_leads.lead: XStreamWireFormat.unmarshalText calls XStream.fromXML on untrusted network data (activemq-http/src/main/java/org/apache/activemq/transport/xstream/XStreamWireFormat.java 64-76), and XmlMessageRenderer uses XStream for output (activemq-web/src/main/java/org/apache/activemq/web/view/XmlMessageRenderer.java 38-46).
rejected_leads.reason: XStream on untrusted input is a known unsafe-deserialization pattern, but this wire format is not enabled by default and no security-relevant converter configuration was in scope to confirm exploitability; lower priority than the default-reachable OpenWire issue.

rejected_leads.lead: LDAPLoginModule.bindUser binds with the user-supplied password without rejecting an empty password (activemq-jaas/src/main/java/org/apache/activemq/jaas/LDAPLoginModule.java 437-456); some LDAP servers treat a bind with a DN and empty password as an unauthenticated/anonymous bind that succeeds, which would allow authentication bypass.
rejected_leads.reason: Conditional on LDAP server behavior and on the LDAP login module being configured; I could not confirm the server-side semantics from source alone, so it remains an unconfirmed lead rather than a candidate.

summary: Apache ActiveMQ 5.15.12 source snapshot (2,691 visible files; test sources and .jspf includes are absent from the snapshot, and no file-name/size/symlink exclusions were applied per get_source_scope). I inspected the remotely reachable transport/unmarshalling paths, broker security/authorization code, the web console (JSP/tags/servlets), JAAS login modules, HTTP/XStream wire formats, and the blob/JDBC stores. The strongest, best-evidenced issue is in the OpenWire marshalling layer: an unauthenticated peer can supply an arbitrary class name inside a serialized Throwable field, and the broker/client instantiates that class through its String constructor with no Throwable-type or allow-list check (createThrowable in every openwire version package). Because unmarshalling happens in the TCP read loop before any broker authentication, this is a pre-auth remote code-execution primitive on the default tcp://0.0.0.0:61616 connector; exploit success is conditional on a suitable class being on the JVM classpath (commonly true in the shipped distribution). I also identified a reflected XSS in the admin console (message.jsp script block, JMSDestination parameter) which I list as a rejected lead because it requires an authenticated console user to follow a crafted link and is lower impact.
